abstract: Evolutionary game theory describes how the frequencies of strategies change in a population when individuals imitate others who have higher payoffs. Models of imitation typically assume that updating is undirected, so that any individual may adopt the strategy of any other. But in many systems some replacements occur in one direction only: in a food chain, for example, a predator species can replace its prey but not the reverse. Here we study replicator dynamics with directed updating rules in a generalized Rock-Paper-Scissor game, in which each strategy can replace only one of the other two. Under undirected updating, increasing the payoff that Paper receives against Rock produces a population in which Scissors is close to fixation. Under directed updating, by contrast, the frequencies of all three strategies oscillate around an interior state. Moreover, when each strategy can replace only the strategy that beats it, increasing the payoff of Paper against Rock decreases the equilibrium frequency of Scissors, which is the opposite of its effect at the Nash equilibrium of the game. This reversal accompanies a reversal in the direction in which the population state rotates around the interior equilibrium. Our results indicate that the direction of strategy updating, and not only the payoff structure of the game, determines which strategies are common at equilibrium.
